preemptive

pree-EMP-tiv -- from Latin prae- ('before') + emere ('to take, buy'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Preemptive is done in advance in order to prevent or forestall something.

The school issued a preemptive announcement about the snow day before the storm had even started.

Example

Rather than wait for customers to complain about the delay, the airline sent a preemptive email apologizing and offering a travel credit.

Taking action ahead of time, specifically to head off a problem before it fully arrives, is exactly what preemptive describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

anticipatory: Anticipatory means done in expectation of something coming -- an anticipatory glance at the door before the guests arrive. A preemptive act goes beyond expecting: it strikes first, specifically to forestall the threat or seize the advantage before the other side can move.

proactive: Proactive describes a general working style -- a proactive manager fixes small problems early, before anyone complains. It names an ongoing habit, never a single strike. A preemptive move is one targeted act, made first, against one specific threat.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reactive: responding only after something has already happened

retaliatory: done in response as payback for something

Where it sits · how directly it targets the threat

precautionary → preemptive → preventive

precautionary vs. preemptive: Precautionary is milder than preemptive: a precautionary test simply guards against risk in general, while a preemptive move strikes first to stop a specific threat before it can begin.

preventive vs. preemptive: Preventive goes further than preemptive: a preemptive move races to get ahead of a specific threat, while a preventive measure -- like regular maintenance on an aging machine -- is designed to stop the problem from ever happening at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-: before (Latin)

root — -empt-: to take, buy (Latin (emere))

suffix — -ive: tending to, having the nature of (Latin (-ivus))

Put it together: Latin pre- ('before') plus emere ('to take, buy') plus -ive ('tending to') -- a preemptive action tends to take the moment first, seizing it before a problem can even arrive.

Use the root in a new word: exempt: Because she'd already passed the certification exam, she was exempt from the retest.
